question: Sébastien Chenu, vice-president of the French National Assembly, was invited to Sciences Po Paris on 19 March to take part in a conference-debate on the role of opposition parties in the National Assembly1. A top university, particularly one of political sciences, is naturally an arena for debate where ideas and political persuasions intersect democratically.

However, this tolerance is not reciprocated by far-left organisations, who appealed for the debate to be called off, or even for it to be violently disrupted. Let us not forget that these same organisations gained infamy for the pro-Palestinian demonstration on 12 March 2024, during which regrettable anti-Semitic ‘incidents’ are reported to have taken place.

Since the Sciences Po website shows that the university is already financed by European institutions such as the European Investment Bank2, would the Commission also be willing to finance further teaching for far-left students at leading European political science schools to familiarise them with democratic principles such as political pluralism, freedom of expression, managing aggressive and violent behaviour, and the fight against anti-Semitism?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.6.2024) According to Article 165 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union1, Member States are exclusively responsible for the content of teaching and organisation of their education systems. The role of the EU is a supporting and coordinating one.

Through the Erasmus+ programme2, the Commission supports higher education institutions across Europe to engage in transnational co-operation, including on citizenship and democracy. The beneficiaries of the Erasmus+ programme have to adhere the EU values of respect for human dignity, freedom, democracy, equality, the rule of law and promotion of human rights.

Supported activities may for example take the form of curriculum development and innovative and new learning methods related to these topics. Participation in the Erasmus+ programme is voluntary and granted on a competitive basis.

Universities located in Erasmus + programme countries, including universities in France, can respond to the annual call and present an application to deliver teaching and learning – as long as they fulfil the related award criteria.
